messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  (none)

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  (none)

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Miguel Alvarez is a 58-year-old forensic analyst who came to treatment nearly a year after an industrial explosion at a municipal evidence storage facility where he had been sent to assist with post-blast identification and scene reconstruction. He still describes the day in sharply sensory fragments: the metallic smell in the air, the pulverized concrete coating his shoes, the sudden secondary bang that sent everyone around him ducking, and the unnerving uncertainty about whether the structure was stable or whether something else had been planted. Because the disaster was caused by human action rather than accident, what stayed with him most was the conviction that danger could be hidden inside ordinary places, waiting behind a locked door or inside a building that looked routine from the outside. He had spent his career entering scenes methodically, trusting procedure and training, and the experience unsettled that trust at its core.

In the weeks afterward, Miguel noticed that his body no longer seemed to stand down. He sat at his desk in the forensic lab with his shoulders tight and jaw clenched, as if bracing for another blast without realizing it until hours had passed. Sudden sounds in the office—a dropped metal tray, a slammed file drawer, the sharp buzz of a security gate—made him jolt hard enough that coworkers began to glance over. He found himself scanning hallways, exits, and unfamiliar faces before he could focus on casework. Even at home, his wife noticed that he seemed wound up, turning quickly toward noises from the street and reacting as though he had been interrupted in the middle of something dangerous.

Miguel had also come to see the world in harsher terms. He was certain now that the world was dangerous, not in an abstract way but in the specific sense that ordinary settings could not be trusted. A warehouse, a parking garage, a courthouse annex—any place he did not know well felt impossible to relax in because he could not assess what might happen there. He began declining invitations that required going somewhere new, telling friends and family that he was tired or busy. When his department rotated assignments to unfamiliar buildings, he tried to trade tasks or asked for floor plans in advance, lingering over entry points and exits in a way that he once would have considered excessive. If he could not picture the space beforehand, he preferred not to go at all. At work this became increasingly noticeable, because forensic analysis occasionally required him to consult on scenes outside his usual lab environment. The prospect of stepping into a new site made his chest tighten before he had even left the office.

What troubled him almost as much as the fear itself was what he believed it said about him. Miguel had always thought of himself as steady, the person younger staff sought out when a case was gruesome or complicated. Now he had come to believe that his reactions proved he was a lousy coper. He judged himself for the way he startled, for how carefully he mapped exits, for the excuses he made to avoid unfamiliar locations. He said with visible shame that other men had been at that disaster too and had “moved on,” while he was still acting like his body had not gotten the message. Beneath that was a deeper loss: he feared he was no longer capable of doing the things that had defined him. He had built an identity around precision, calm, and competence under pressure, and it felt humiliating to wonder whether that version of himself was gone.

Over the following months, these beliefs narrowed his life. Miguel kept to predictable routes, familiar restaurants, and the same grocery store aisle pattern, not because these routines gave him pleasure but because they reduced the strain of having to judge an unknown environment. His wife wanted to take weekend trips, but he resisted anywhere he had not been before. In the lab, he remained highly knowledgeable and meticulous, yet he increasingly tried to stay with bench analysis rather than field-related duties. He noticed this retreat and interpreted it as further evidence that he was diminished, which left him more discouraged and more preoccupied with how unsafe everything felt. Even small disruptions—construction noise outside the building, an alarm test, a stranger entering a secure area unexpectedly—could leave him keyed up for hours.

By the time Miguel sought help, the strain had become difficult to hide. A recent assignment to review evidence in an unfamiliar county facility left him so tense beforehand that he barely slept, and when a metal cart crashed in the corridor he recoiled so sharply that a junior colleague asked if he was all right. That moment embarrassed him more than he expected. He came in saying he was tired of feeling on edge and tired of arranging his life around places he could not fully control. What frightened him most was the possibility that this was simply who he was now: a man no longer able to trust the world, or himself. What he hopes for, cautiously, is not to erase what happened but to walk into a new place without feeling his whole body prepare for disaster.
